findings.recommendation: Replace the literal with the same indirection the `docs` server already uses on rag-agent/config/mcp.json:11 -- `"BILLING_API_KEY": "${BILLING_API_KEY}"` -- and inject the value from a secrets manager at launch. Treat the committed key as compromised: revoke and reissue it, then purge it from git history, and add a pre-commit/CI secret scanner so a literal sk- value cannot be committed again.

findings.title: aws_security_group.admin exposes bastion SSH (port 22) to 0.0.0.0/0
findings.evidence:
The bastion security group, described in the file as `operator access to the bastion` (line 3), opens TCP/22 to the entire internet: `from_port = 22`, `to_port = 22`, `protocol = "tcp"`, `cidr_blocks = ["0.0.0.0/0"]` (lines 7-10). The attacker-controlled input is an unauthenticated TCP connection from any source address on the internet to port 22 of any instance in this group; it is accepted at line 10, which is the only rule deciding who may reach sshd. The sibling resource in the same file establishes the intended distinction: `aws_security_group.public_alb` is described as `internet-facing load balancer` (line 16) and opens 0.0.0.0/0 on 443 (lines 19-24) -- that is a service designed for anonymous internet traffic terminating TLS. A bastion for named operators is the opposite case, and it carries the same CIDR. The bastion is by definition the pivot into the private subnets, so the group with the widest exposure is the one guarding the highest-value hop.

Independent validation: modules/network/main.tf:6-11 opens tcp/22 with cidr_blocks = ["0.0.0.0/0"] (line 10) on the group whose own description is 'operator access to the bastion' (line 3): the entire internet can reach the bastion's SSH listener, with no prior access required (rule 13 ingress = any host on the internet at line 10). Rule 10: stripped modules/network/main.tf:14 - aws_security_group.public_alb serving 443 from 0.0.0.0/0 is the intended contract for an internet-facing load balancer and must not be flagged.

Production viability (VIABLE): The bastion security group opens TCP/22 to 0.0.0.0/0 in the network module as written, and the public_alb sibling in the same file shows the internet-facing exception was applied deliberately elsewhere - this rule ships as the operator access path.
findings.impact: Every sshd on the bastion tier is reachable by the entire internet: continuous credential brute-force and password-spray against operator accounts, immediate exploitation window for any OpenSSH pre-authentication vulnerability, and host-key/version fingerprinting for targeting. A successful login or exploit yields a foothold inside the VPC -- from which the worker instance credentials described in the root module (`Action = "*"` on `Resource = "*"`) become reachable.
findings.recommendation: Replace `["0.0.0.0/0"]` on line 10 with a variable holding the operator office/VPN egress prefixes, keeping the blanket CIDR only for the genuinely internet-facing listener as `aws_security_group.public_alb` does on line 23. Better still, remove the ingress rule entirely and reach instances through AWS Systems Manager Session Manager or EC2 Instance Connect Endpoint, which need no inbound port at all; if the bastion must stay, additionally disable password authentication on sshd so the exposed port cannot be brute-forced.

findings.title: Unverified JWT in currentUser lets any caller forge sub and role in lib/auth.js
findings.evidence:
lib/auth.js:4 resolves the request identity from the raw Authorization header: line 5 strips the 'Bearer ' prefix off `req.headers.authorization`, and line 6 calls `const claims = jwt.decode(bearer);`. `jwt.decode` parses the base64 payload and returns it WITHOUT checking the signature or any registered claim; only `jwt.verify(token, key, opts)` does that, and jsonwebtoken 9.0.2 (package.json:8) exposes it. Line 7 then returns `{ id: claims && claims.sub, role: claims && claims.role }` straight to the handlers, so the whole identity of the request -- the tenant id used as the owner binding in the SQL of routes/invoices.js:16, :24 and :32, and the privilege label `role` -- is a value the caller typed. An unauthenticated internet caller (THREAT_MODEL A1) mints `eyJhbGciOiJub25lIn0.<base64 of {"sub":"<victim>","role":"admin","tenant":"<victim>"}>.` with no key at all and is that user. The same module shows the intended contract one function down: `tagRequest` feeds the decoded token only into a metrics label at line 13 and returns the server-held `req.session.user` (line 14) as the actual caller, i.e. the trusted identity in this codebase comes from the session, not from the bearer token. THREAT_MODEL lists 'identity asserted by a client-supplied header or an unverified JWT' as highest-risk interface #1, and kb/entities/authorization.md records this exact defect: 'lib/auth.js resolves the caller with jwt.decode (no verify)'.

Independent validation: lib/auth.js:6 calls jwt.decode(bearer), which parses the token without verifying its signature, and line 7 returns claims.sub and claims.role as the caller's identity and role. Rule 13 ingress: lib/auth.js:5, the client-supplied Authorization header. jsonwebtoken is a declared dependency (package.json:8) and exposes jwt.verify, so this is the unsafe member of a safe API, not a library limitation. The sibling tagRequest also decodes at line 12 but uses it only as a metrics label and returns req.session.user, so it is not the security-relevant call; code_path narrowed accordingly.

Production viability (CONDITIONAL_VIABLE): jwt.decode without verification is a complete defect in the shipped helper, but lib/auth.js has no in-tree importer and the middleware that populates the req.user the routes consume is absent from this slice.
findings.impact: Complete authentication and tenant-isolation bypass with no credential. Any unauthenticated caller sets `sub` to any tenant id and reads that tenant's invoices, receipts and payments through the owner-bound queries (which now bind the attacker's chosen owner), and sets `role` to any privileged value the application trusts. Every owner_id predicate in the service, including the one that makes /receipts/:id look safe, is neutralised by a forged token.
findings.recommendation: Replace `jwt.decode(bearer)` at lib/auth.js:6 with `jwt.verify(bearer, PUBLIC_KEY_OR_SECRET, { algorithms: ['RS256'], issuer, audience })` inside a try/catch that rejects the request on any error, so an absent, expired, wrong-issuer or `alg: none` token yields no identity instead of an attacker-chosen one. Follow the pattern the sibling `tagRequest` (lib/auth.js:11-15) already demonstrates: derive the authoritative caller from the server-held session (`req.session.user`, line 14) and let the decoded token supply only non-authoritative labels such as the metrics tenant tag.

findings.title: _caller_may_export in routes_exports.py ignores caller_id and authorizes every existing export record
findings.evidence:
GET /exports/<record_id> (routes_exports.py:16) calls fetch_export(record_id) with the caller-supplied path segment and then gates on _caller_may_export(record, request.headers.get("X-Caller")). The predicate at routes_exports.py:10 accepts caller_id and never references it; after the None guard the decisive line is `return True` (routes_exports.py:13). The untrusted input is the <record_id> path segment of any GET /exports/<id>; it reaches fetch_export at routes_exports.py:18 and the predicate at line 13 approves whatever came back. Exports are the highest-value object in this service because the threat model flags 'whole-object serialization of a PII-bearing record' as a top interface, and routes_exports.py:21 does exactly that with jsonify(record). The shipped docker-compose.yml:6 also raises EXPORT_PAGE_SIZE to "100", double the 50 baked into the Dockerfile and .env.example, so each unauthorized read returns twice the rows the image default intended.

Independent validation: Confirmed independently at intake-portal/app/routes_exports.py:10-13: _caller_may_export(record, caller_id) accepts caller_id and never reads it, returning True for any non-None record, so the sole gate is record existence and any caller reads any export record. Untrusted ingress is the request itself: the record-id path segment on the route declared at intake-portal/app/routes_exports.py:16 and the caller header at intake-portal/app/routes_exports.py:19, both wholly client-controlled. The dict-backed _ROWS at store.py:10 is a stand-in for the real store the same module wires up (psycopg2 _connect() at store.py:13-14 over DATABASE_URL, with the Postgres service at docker-compose.yml:10-14), not a mock that makes the flaw unreachable; the hardened twin routes_admin.py:13 (record["owner_id"] == caller_id) proves the intended contract this module deviates from.

Production viability (CONDITIONAL_VIABLE): _caller_may_export authorizes any existing export record as written, but fetch_export resolves against store.py's dict-backed stand-in that no code populates, so the PII-bearing export leak needs the real store behind it.
findings.impact: An unauthenticated caller enumerating export ids downloads other tenants' bulk PII exports in full. This is the widest data-egress path in the service: one weak predicate converts every generated export into a public object.
findings.recommendation: Port the ownership comparison from the hardened twin _caller_may_edit (intake-portal/app/routes_admin.py:13) -- `return record["owner_id"] == caller_id` -- and additionally scope the export at the query layer so a non-owner id never materialises a record. Depends on replacing the X-Caller header identity (see routes_admin.py:19 finding).

findings.title: verify_partner_signature computes the expected HMAC and discards it, returning True for any non-empty signature
findings.evidence:
security.py:10 defines verify_partner_signature(payload, signature). Line 12 computes `expected = hmac.new(SIGNING_KEY, payload, hashlib.sha256).hexdigest()`, line 13-14 reject only the empty/None case, and the decisive line 15 is `return True`. `expected` is never compared to anything -- the local is dead. The untrusted inputs are the partner webhook body (payload) and the partner-supplied signature header value (signature); both land in this function and the function returns True at security.py:15 for every payload as long as the signature string is non-empty. The intended contract is written out five lines below in the hardened twin verify_internal_token, whose body is otherwise identical and which ends at security.py:21 with `return hmac.compare_digest(expected, signature)`. The presence of the correct comparison in the twin, over the same key and the same digest, is what makes line 15 a defect rather than an unimplemented stub.

Independent validation: security.py:12 computes `expected` and security.py:13-15 then throws it away: the function returns True for any non-empty signature string, so the HMAC is never compared and every partner webhook with a non-blank signature header authenticates. The correct sibling in the same file, verify_internal_token at security.py:21, does hmac.compare_digest(expected, signature), which establishes the intended contract. This is an intrinsic broken authentication algorithm (rule 08), valid even though no in-tree caller wires it; the untrusted input is the partner-supplied signature the docstring at security.py:11 describes.

Production viability (CONDITIONAL_VIABLE): verify_partner_signature discarding `expected` and returning True is unconditional in the shipped helper, but no module in this tree imports security.py, so the partner webhook route that would consume the bypass is absent from the slice.
findings.impact: Any unauthenticated internet caller forges partner webhook deliveries: send an arbitrary body with a header such as `X-Signature: x` and it verifies. The partner webhook is the service's trust boundary for partner-asserted state, so this yields authenticated-partner write capability without possessing PARTNER_SIGNING_KEY at all.
findings.recommendation: Return the constant-time comparison that the hardened twin verify_internal_token already uses at intake-portal/app/security.py:21: `return hmac.compare_digest(expected, signature)`. Keep the empty-signature guard, and make the function total (no early True). A unit test asserting that a wrong signature returns False would have caught this.

findings.title: customer_response serializes the whole Customer dataclass, exposing national_id, internal_risk_score and support_notes in the dashboard JSON
findings.evidence:
app/serializers.py turns the record into the API body with no field allowlist. The decisive line is analytics-service/app/serializers.py:18 -- `return asdict(customer)` -- and `asdict` walks every field declared on the dataclass at lines 8-13, so `national_id` (line 11), `internal_risk_score` (line 12) and `support_notes` (line 13) are placed in the response served to whoever the dashboard request authenticates as (threat-model actor A2, an authenticated but unprivileged tenant). Two of those three are internal-only by their own names: a risk score computed for internal decisioning and free-text notes staff write about the customer. The intended contract is stated a few lines below: `PUBLIC_FIELDS = ("id", "email", "full_name")` (line 21) and `customer_response_public` (line 24), whose docstring notes a test fails when a new field appears. The weak variant has the opposite failure mode -- because it enumerates fields dynamically, any field added to Customer later is published automatically and silently.

Independent validation: serializers.py:18 returns asdict(customer) for the customer-facing dashboard, so every field of the dataclass declared at lines 6-13 -- national_id, internal_risk_score and support_notes -- ships in the API response; the sibling customer_response_public (lines 21-26) projects only PUBLIC_FIELDS ('id','email','full_name'). Internal-only fields crossing to the client is excessive data exposure (CWE-213), a security finding rather than a compliance one, and the flaw is intrinsic to the function (rule 08). MEDIUM stands.

Production viability (VIABLE): customer_response returns asdict(customer), which emits national_id, internal_risk_score and support_notes with no allowlist; PUBLIC_FIELDS exists in the same file and is simply not used by this shipped serializer.
findings.impact: An ordinary authenticated dashboard user reads internal data the product never meant to show them: the internal risk score driving decisions on their account and the free-text support notes written about them, which routinely contain third-party detail and staff assessments. The national ID also ends up in a JSON body that browsers, intermediate caches and proxy logs retain. Any future field added to the record -- a fraud flag, an auth token, an internal comment -- leaks the moment it is declared, with no code change to this function.
findings.recommendation: Serve the dashboard from the hardened twin customer_response_public (analytics-service/app/serializers.py:24), which projects only PUBLIC_FIELDS, and delete customer_response so no route can reach asdict() on a PII-bearing record. Keep the test that fails when a new dataclass field is not classified, so the allowlist stays the only way a field becomes public.

findings.title: CertificatesStats.get returns system-wide counts_by_month with no tenant scoping while its own post sibling is authority-gated
findings.evidence:
CertificatesStats inherits AuthenticatedResource, which by its own docstring grants "a session ... not any role" (resources.py:8). Its read handler is `return service.counts_by_month()` (resources.py:40) - no `current_user()`, no permission object, no argument narrowing the result to the caller's tenant. The attacker input is the authenticated request itself (any valid session cookie, from any tenant, with zero roles) aimed at this route; it lands at resources.py:40 and returns the global aggregate. Two hardened references bracket it. First, the same verb on the sibling resource IS scoped: CertificatesList.get is `return service.list_for(service.current_user())` (resources.py:15). Second, the other half of this very class IS gated: CertificatesStats.post builds `AuthorityPermission(data["authority"].id, service.current_user().roles)` and 403s (resources.py:43-45) before recomputing statistics for one authority. So the code treats per-authority statistics as privileged when writing them and as public when reading them.

Independent validation: api/resources.py:40 returns service.counts_by_month() with no argument, while the analogous read on the sibling resource passes the principal explicitly - service.list_for(service.current_user()) at line 15 - and this same class's post is authority-gated at lines 43-45. That explicit-principal convention throughout the file argues against implicit scoping inside the service layer, so the aggregate is cross-tenant. Rule 13: the untrusted principal is any authenticated user, since api/resources.py:8 states a session implies no role. MEDIUM retained - it exposes aggregate issuance volume only, no records or PII. Caveat: service.py is not in the tree, so the unscoped shape rests on the zero-argument call against a scoped sibling.

Production viability (VIABLE): CertificatesStats.get returns service.counts_by_month() with no current_user() narrowing in the code that ships, and any roleless authenticated session reaches it in a standard build.
findings.impact: Any authenticated, unprivileged tenant reads certificate issuance volume for the entire platform broken down by month - a cross-tenant business-intelligence leak (total customer/certificate scale, growth rate, and issuance spikes that correlate with other tenants' deployments and incidents). It also serves as reconnaissance confirming that unscoped queries exist behind this session, and, because it recomputes nothing, it is a cheap oracle for observing the effect of the supersede and upload abuses above.
findings.recommendation: Scope the read the way the hardened twin CertificatesList.get does (resources.py:15): pass `service.current_user()` into the aggregate, e.g. `service.counts_by_month(service.current_user())`, so the figures cover only the caller's own certificates. If a platform-wide view is genuinely wanted, gate it with the same AuthorityPermission the post half of this class already applies (resources.py:43-45), or with an explicit admin role - the base resource grants none.

findings.title: ingest_ticket indexes raw customer ticket bodies with no origin or trust metadata, leaving retrieval unable to filter untrusted text
findings.evidence:
agent/memory.py:28 is `index.add_texts([ticket["body"]])`. `ticket["body"]` is text an A3 content author typed into a support ticket; it crosses into the retrieval corpus carrying nothing -- no origin, no trust level, not even the ticket id. Once stored this way the chunk is indistinguishable from curated first-party documentation, so no downstream retrieval filter can exclude or downrank it and no prompt builder can label it: build_prompt (agent/answer.py:13) receives it as a bare string in list[str], and even build_prompt_marked (agent/answer.py:16) cannot mark it, because line 21 reads `d['origin']` and `d['trust']` -- fields this ingestion path never wrote. The hardened twin immediately below, ingest_ticket_marked (agent/memory.py:31), states the contract and even names the consumer in its docstring: it passes `metadatas=[{"origin": "customer-ticket", "trust": "untrusted", "ticket_id": ticket["id"]}]` (line 35), 'which retrieval filters on'.

Independent validation: memory.py:28 calls index.add_texts([ticket['body']]) with no metadatas, so customer-authored ticket text enters the retrieval corpus indistinguishable from trusted material; the sibling ingest_ticket_marked (memory.py:31-36) attaches origin/trust and build_prompt_marked reads exactly those d['origin']/d['trust'] keys at answer.py:21, so documents ingested here cannot be filtered by -- or even rendered on -- the safe path. This is the untrusted ingress leg of the chain that ends at the sinks in answer.py:30 and :48, not a hygiene nit. MEDIUM is right.

Production viability (VIABLE): ingest_ticket indexes the raw ticket body with no metadata, and the module's own ingest_ticket_marked plus answer.build_prompt_marked prove the metadata fields downstream filters need are simply never written by this shipped path.
findings.impact: Attacker-authored ticket text is permanently promoted to trusted-corpus status. This is the storage half of the indirect-injection chain: it guarantees that the marked prompt builder degrades to the unmarked one and that trust-based retrieval filtering cannot be enforced later, so a single filed ticket can steer every future answer that retrieves it -- and through it the refund path at agent/answer.py:30 and the shell path at agent/answer.py:48.
findings.recommendation: Ingest exclusively through the hardened twin ingest_ticket_marked (rag-agent/agent/memory.py:31) so every chunk carries origin, trust and ticket_id, and make the metadata mandatory at the index layer so a call without it fails closed. Then have retrieval filter or downrank trust='untrusted' chunks and have the prompt builder render them in delimited document blocks.

findings.title: The billing MCP server is auto-installed from the mutable @latest tag via npx -y, executing unreviewed code with the billing key in its environment
findings.evidence:
config/mcp.json:5 is `"args": ["-y", "@acme/billing-mcp@latest"]`. `-y` suppresses npx's install confirmation and `@latest` is a mutable dist-tag, so every agent start resolves and executes whatever tarball the registry serves for that tag at that moment -- there is no version pin, no integrity/digest pin and no lockfile in this config. The attacker-controlled input is the published package contents: anyone who obtains publish rights on @acme/billing-mcp (compromised maintainer token, or a dependency-confusion publish if the @acme scope is not owned on the public registry) changes what this line runs, and npm lifecycle scripts execute at install time before any agent logic runs. The effect is compounded by the very next line: line 6 hands that process a live BILLING_API_KEY. The sibling `docs` server on lines 9-10 shows the safe shape -- `"command": "node", "args": ["./servers/docs/index.js"]` -- a local, reviewed, in-tree entry point with nothing fetched at run time.

Independent validation: config/mcp.json:5 runs "npx" with args ["-y", "@acme/billing-mcp@latest"], so a mutable tag is resolved and executed at every start with no review step, no lockfile and no install confirmation, and line 6 injects the billing credential into that process's environment; the sibling docs server (lines 9-10) runs a pinned local path, so the file itself demonstrates the safer pattern. Verified in-file, but exploitation turns on registry state (a malicious or hijacked publish of that package) rather than a directly triggerable flaw in this repo, so I lowered the finder's HIGH to MEDIUM.

Production viability (VIABLE): `npx -y @acme/billing-mcp@latest` is the shipped launch configuration: every agent start resolves a mutable dist-tag and runs its lifecycle scripts with BILLING_API_KEY in the environment, with no pin or lockfile anywhere in this config.
findings.impact: Supply-chain code execution on the agent host: a single malicious publish to the @acme/billing-mcp tag runs attacker code as the agent user on every start, with BILLING_API_KEY already in its environment and ANTHROPIC_API_KEY in the parent process. Because @latest is mutable, the compromise can also be un-published afterwards, leaving no pinned version to point at during incident response.
findings.recommendation: Vendor the billing server the way the `docs` server is already vendored (rag-agent/config/mcp.json:9-10): a local, reviewed entry point invoked directly, with dependencies resolved from a committed lockfile. If it must stay remote, replace `@latest` with an exact version plus an integrity hash, install it ahead of time with `npm ci --ignore-scripts` instead of `npx -y`, and run the server under a separate least-privilege identity so a compromised build does not inherit the billing key.

findings.title: aws_s3_bucket_public_access_block.reports disables all four public-access guardrails on the billing reports bucket
findings.evidence:
The billing reports bucket `acme-billing-reports-${var.env}` (main.tf line 10) is paired with a public access block whose every control is explicitly turned off: `block_public_acls = false` (line 15), `block_public_policy = false` (line 16), `ignore_public_acls = false` (line 17), `restrict_public_buckets = false` (line 18). These four settings are the account/bucket-level backstop that makes a public ACL or a public bucket policy on this bucket un-applyable and, where one already exists, un-honoured. With all four false, a single `s3:PutBucketAcl` with `public-read`, or a `s3:PutBucketPolicy` with `Principal: "*"`, immediately makes every object world-readable, and the request that lands the data is an unauthenticated `GET https://acme-billing-reports-<env>.s3.amazonaws.com/<key>`. The grant is one API call away from any principal that can touch the bucket -- notably the `worker` role in this same file, whose inline policy is `Action = "*"` on `Resource = "*"` (line 49). The same file shows the intended contract for a bucket that really is served to the public: `aws_s3_bucket.public_site` is never made public by ACL at all -- it is fronted by CloudFront and its policy (lines 29-40) allows only `s3:GetObject` to the specific origin access identity principal `aws_cloudfront_origin_access_identity.site.iam_arn`. The bucket holding billing data is the one with the guardrails removed; the marketing bucket is the one kept private at the origin.

Independent validation: main.tf:13-19 sets all four guardrails (block_public_acls line 15, block_public_policy 16, ignore_public_acls 17, restrict_public_buckets 18) to false on the billing reports bucket declared at main.tf:9-11. That is an affirmative disable of a control AWS enables by default, not an omitted hardening step, and the worker role in the same root holds Action "*" on Resource "*" (main.tf:49-50), so any principal on that path can make the billing reports public with nothing left to block it. Rule 10: stripped main.tf:29 - aws_s3_bucket_policy.public_site is the OAI-restricted correct sibling on a different bucket.

Production viability (VIABLE): All four public-access guardrails on the billing reports bucket are explicitly false in the applied configuration, so a single public ACL or bucket policy takes effect with nothing to block or ignore it.
findings.impact: Billing report objects -- customer billing records and the PII they carry -- become readable by any unauthenticated internet caller or public-bucket scanner as soon as a public ACL or policy is set, and nothing in the configuration prevents that grant from being set. It also removes the containment that would otherwise limit the blast radius of a compromised worker credential or a leaked CI token to authenticated access only.
findings.recommendation: Set all four attributes to `true` on `aws_s3_bucket_public_access_block.reports` (they default to true in AWS's account-level setting and are only being overridden here), and grant read access the way the hardened sibling in this same file does: an explicit `aws_s3_bucket_policy` naming the exact consuming principal, as `aws_s3_bucket_policy.public_site` (lines 29-40) does with the CloudFront origin access identity ARN. Add the account-level `aws_s3_account_public_access_block` so no future bucket can opt out.

findings.title: unpack() calls tarfile.extractall without a member filter, letting archive member paths escape the destination
findings.evidence:
THREAT_MODEL declares 'archive member paths' explicitly UNTRUSTED. unpack() opens a caller-supplied tarball and hands it straight to the extractor with no member vetting: line 18 is `tf.extractall(dest)` -- no `filter=` argument, no per-member path check, no rejection of absolute names, `..` components, symlinks, hardlinks or device nodes. On a Python where the default extraction filter is not yet 'data' this reproduces the classic tar-slip: a member named `../../../../etc/cron.d/packer` or an absolute `/etc/sudoers.d/x`, or a symlink member pointing at a root-owned path followed by a regular member that writes through it, is written wherever the member name says, not under `dest`. main() reaches this function directly with attacker-chosen values: line 92 is `unpack(args.value, ".")`, so the archive path is a bare CLI argument and the destination is the current working directory. Because the README documents the tool as being run under `sudo`, the extraction happens with root's credentials, so nothing on the filesystem constrains the write. The hardened twin sits four lines below and differs by exactly one keyword: unpack_safely() at line 24 calls `tf.extractall(dest, filter="data")`, which is the intended contract for a bundle 'received from the registry'.

Independent validation: packer.py:18 calls tf.extractall(dest) with no filter, so member names carrying '../' or absolute paths are honoured (CVE-2007-4559 / Zip-Slip) on any interpreter where 'data' is not already the default; the sibling unpack_safely passes filter='data' at line 24. Ingress (rule 13): the archive is attacker-supplied and the path is actually wired -- main() parses argv at packer.py:90 and calls unpack(args.value, '.') at line 92, with the member names entering at tarfile.open(archive) on line 17. Arbitrary file write as the invoking user; HIGH stands. Refined code_paths per rule 10: dropped line 24, the correct sibling.

Production viability (VIABLE): unpack() is the one command main() actually dispatches (packer.py:91-92), and tarfile.extractall with no filter= still defaults to fully-trusted extraction on current Python runtimes, so a hostile member path escapes dest as written.
findings.impact: An attacker who supplies or tampers with a bundle gets an arbitrary-path file write outside the destination directory. Run under the documented sudo path this is a root-owned write to any location -- dropping a cron entry, a sudoers rule, an SSH authorized_keys or replacing a binary on PATH -- i.e. full host compromise from a single malicious archive. Without sudo it is still arbitrary overwrite of the invoking user's files.
findings.recommendation: Use the hardened twin already present in this file: unpack_safely() (packer.py:21-24), which passes `filter="data"` to extractall. Either route the `unpack` CLI command at line 92 to unpack_safely(), or add `filter="data"` to line 18 and delete the weak variant. `filter="data"` rejects absolute paths, `..` escapes, links pointing outside the destination, and special files. If an older interpreter must be supported, resolve each member name against the realpath of dest and skip anything that does not stay inside it, plus skip members where `not member.isreg() and not member.isdir()`.

findings.title: Missing owner predicate in GET /invoices/:id returns any tenant's invoice
findings.evidence:
routes/invoices.js:7 handles the invoice detail screen and builds its query at line 8: `const invoice = await db.query('SELECT * FROM invoices WHERE id = $1', [req.params.id]);`. The only predicate is the row id, which is the attacker-controlled path segment `req.params.id`. Nothing in the handler references `req.user`, so no owner, tenant or role is ever compared against the row before line 9 serialises the whole record with `res.json(invoice)`. The hardened twin sits six lines below and does the same job for the same billing screen: /receipts/:id at routes/invoices.js:13 queries `'SELECT * FROM receipts WHERE id = $1 AND owner_id = $2'` with `[req.params.id, req.user.id]` (lines 15-16), binding the caller as a second predicate. The two detail endpoints are written to the same shape and differ only in that owner binding, which is the evidence that binding the owner is the intended contract; kb/entities/authorization.md records the same asymmetry: '/invoices/:id has no owner predicate; /receipts/:id binds owner_id = $2'. The asymmetry also changes who can reach each route: /receipts/:id dereferences `req.user.id` and therefore fails for a caller with no session, while /invoices/:id never touches `req.user` and answers an anonymous request. Enumerating or guessing sequential invoice ids walks the whole table. Because `SELECT *` is returned unfiltered, every column of the billing record crosses the boundary (THREAT_MODEL highest-risk interface #5, whole-object serialization of a PII-bearing record).

Independent validation: routes/invoices.js:8 issues SELECT * FROM invoices WHERE id = $1 bound to req.params.id with no owner predicate and returns the row to any caller, while the hardened twin five lines down at routes/invoices.js:15 proves the intended contract with AND owner_id = $2 bound to req.user.id. Rule 13 ingress: the client-controlled path segment req.params.id at line 8, on the route declared at line 7. lib/db.js:2 is a declared stand-in, but the defect is the SQL predicate composed in the route itself, which is fully decidable from the text and independent of the driver behind it.

Production viability (CONDITIONAL_VIABLE): The missing owner predicate is in the query string the route ships, and the hardened /receipts/:id twin six lines below proves the contract, but lib/db.js is a two-line stand-in returning [] so no row is actually disclosed until the real client is behind it.
findings.impact: Cross-tenant read of arbitrary invoice records by id, with no session required. An attacker iterating :id harvests other tenants' billing rows in full -- amounts, customer identifiers and every other column of the invoices table -- which is exactly the question THREAT_MODEL poses for profile A2 and, because the handler never dereferences req.user, is also available to the unauthenticated A1 caller.
findings.recommendation: Add the owner predicate to the query at routes/invoices.js:8 so the row is selected by id AND caller, copying the hardened twin /receipts/:id at routes/invoices.js:15: `db.query('SELECT * FROM invoices WHERE id = $1 AND owner_id = $2', [req.params.id, req.user.id])`, and return 404 (not 403) on no rows so the endpoint does not confirm the existence of other tenants' ids. Enforce the presence of an authenticated `req.user` in middleware ahead of the router so the route cannot answer an anonymous request, and note that the predicate is only worth anything once lib/auth.js:6 verifies the token signature.

findings.title: SQL injection via the order query parameter interpolated into ORDER BY in GET /invoices
findings.evidence:
routes/invoices.js:22 lists invoices for the table header's sort control. Line 23 takes the sort key straight off the query string with no validation -- `const order = req.query.order || 'created_at';` -- and line 24 splices that string into the statement text with a template literal: ``await db.query(`SELECT * FROM invoices WHERE owner_id = $1 ORDER BY ${order}`, [req.user.id])``. Only the owner id travels as a bound parameter; `order` becomes SQL source. ORDER BY is not parameterisable, which is precisely why it must be allowlisted rather than interpolated, and the sibling endpoint does exactly that: /payments at routes/invoices.js:30 maps the caller's `req.query.sort` through the fixed dictionary `const SORTABLE = { date: 'created_at', amount: 'total_cents' };` declared at line 29 and interpolates only `SORTABLE[req.query.sort] || SORTABLE.date` (line 31-32), so no attacker byte can reach the statement. Two list endpoints, the same job, one safe. A request such as `GET /invoices?order=(SELECT CASE WHEN (SELECT current_setting('is_superuser'))='on' THEN 1 ELSE 1/0 END)` or `?order=1--` reaches the parser; the trailing position after ORDER BY accepts subqueries, so a boolean- or error-based oracle extracts arbitrary rows from any table the connection can read, and a driver permitting stacked statements would take a second statement outright.

Independent validation: routes/invoices.js:23 takes req.query.order straight from the query string and line 24 interpolates it into the SQL template as ORDER BY ${order}: the owner_id value is bound as $1 but the ORDER BY fragment is not parameterised at all, so the attacker's text is concatenated into the statement. I confirmed the finding is on the unparameterised route and not its sibling: /payments at line 31 maps req.query.sort through the server-authored SORTABLE allow-list declared at line 29 and falls back to SORTABLE.date, so `column` can only ever be one of two literals - that sibling is safe and I did not stretch to it (rule 05). Rule 13 ingress: routes/invoices.js:23.

Production viability (CONDITIONAL_VIABLE): The `order` query parameter is spliced into the statement text at routes/invoices.js:24 exactly as it would ship, but lib/db.js is a two-line stand-in whose query() returns [] without executing, so the injected SQL runs only against the real pg client it replaces.
findings.impact: Attacker-controlled SQL executed with the application's database privileges. Via subselects in the ORDER BY position the attacker exfiltrates rows the owner_id predicate was supposed to fence off -- other tenants' invoices, payments and receipts -- and reads any other table the billing role can reach; the same oracle enumerates the schema. Where stacked statements are permitted the injection extends to writes.
findings.recommendation: Never interpolate `req.query.order` into the statement. Resolve it through a server-side allowlist exactly as the hardened twin /payments does with the `SORTABLE` map at routes/invoices.js:29-32: map the caller's key to a fixed column identifier, fall back to a default on an unknown key, and validate the direction against the literal set ['ASC','DESC']. Reject rather than silently default if the audit trail matters.

findings.title: middleware.allow read-modify-writes the package-global buckets map with no lock, so concurrent requests trip Go's fatal concurrent map write and abort the gateway
findings.evidence:
The rate limiter's entire state is a bare map declared at middleware/limits.go:40, `var buckets = map[string]int{}` - no sync.Mutex, no sync.RWMutex, no sync.Map. `allow` reads it at middleware/limits.go:29 (`bucket, ok := buckets[key]`) and writes it at the decisive line middleware/limits.go:36, `buckets[key] = bucket - 1`. net/http serves every connection on its own goroutine, so each request passing through `Throttle` (middleware/limits.go:18-26) enters this unsynchronised read-modify-write in parallel with every other. Go maps are explicitly not safe for concurrent use: the runtime's hashWriting flag detection aborts the whole process with `fatal error: concurrent map writes` / `concurrent map read and map write`, which is a runtime throw, not a panic - `recover()` cannot intercept it and no handler-level middleware can contain it. The untrusted input is simply the arrival rate and concurrency of requests from an unauthenticated A1 caller, i.e. precisely the condition this middleware exists to survive; two overlapping requests are sufficient. The same missing lock also makes the check itself wrong under load: two goroutines can both read the same `bucket` value at limits.go:29 and both write `bucket - 1` at limits.go:36, so decrements are lost and the burst ceiling is not actually enforced. Reachability, stated plainly: `Throttle` is exported and is the package's only rate limiter, but the public table in router/routes.go wraps no route in it today - routes.go:11 records that the authenticated surface lives in router/private.go, which is not in this tree, so the crash is reachable through whichever route table wires Throttle.

Independent validation: allow() reads buckets[key] at middleware/limits.go:29 and writes buckets[key] at line 36 on the package-global map declared at line 40, with no mutex and no sync.Map, while Throttle (line 18) is HTTP middleware that Go runs in one goroutine per request: concurrent requests hit Go's unrecoverable runtime throw 'concurrent map writes', which defer/recover cannot catch and which kills the whole gateway process. Rule 03 explicitly preserves races that can be automated and retried, and two parallel requests suffice. Rule 07 side: not resource exhaustion and not a missing bound - a concurrency/memory-safety defect (CWE-362). Rule 13 ingress: any two concurrent client requests through Throttle at line 20; same caller caveat as its sibling - Throttle is not registered in router/routes.go, so it stands on rule 08 as intrinsic.

Production viability (CONDITIONAL_VIABLE): The unsynchronised read-modify-write of the package-global buckets map is unconditional once concurrent, but allow() is reachable only through middleware.Throttle, which no visible route registers (router/private.go is absent from the slice).
findings.impact: Any caller whose requests reach a Throttle-wrapped route can kill the entire gateway process - an unrecoverable runtime abort that drops every in-flight connection - by doing nothing more exotic than issuing requests in parallel. Where it does not crash, lost decrements silently raise the effective burst limit above the configured value.
findings.recommendation: Perform the lookup, the ceiling test and the decrement inside one critical section guarded by a sync.Mutex held over limits.go:29-36, or replace the hand-rolled counter with a mutex-protected map (or sync.Map) of golang.org/x/time/rate.Limiter values. The hardened sibling in the same file, BodyLimit (middleware/limits.go:10-15), is correct precisely because it touches no shared state - it is the evidence that this package's lock-free middleware style is only safe without a mutable global.

findings.title: Caller identity across all four route modules is the unauthenticated client-supplied X-Caller header
findings.evidence:
Every route module in this package derives the caller from `request.headers.get("X-Caller")` and nothing else -- routes_forms.py:19, routes_partners.py:19, routes_exports.py:19 and routes_admin.py:19. There is no session, no signature and no token validation anywhere on the request path: nothing in this package calls tokens.issue, verify_partner_signature or verify_internal_token before the predicate runs. The decisive line is routes_admin.py:19, `if not _caller_may_edit(record, request.headers.get("X-Caller")):`, because routes_admin.py is the single module whose predicate actually consumes the value (routes_admin.py:13 compares it to record["owner_id"]). The untrusted input is the raw X-Caller request header, chosen freely by the client; it is passed straight into the authorization decision at line 19. The one genuine ownership check in the service is therefore satisfied by typing the victim's owner id into a header, which the attacker learns for free from the unauthorized reads on /forms, /exports and /partners.

Independent validation: routes_admin.py:19 reads request.headers.get("X-Caller") and feeds it straight into the ownership comparison at routes_admin.py:13; an HTTP request header is entirely client-authored and nothing in the tree authenticates it - tokens.py:11-12 mints bearer tokens but no route module imports or consumes them, and none of the four blueprints applies a session, signature or token check. So the one module that does compare owner_id is still bypassed by sending X-Caller: <victim owner_id>. Rule 13 ingress: routes_admin.py:19. This is a distinct defect from the three ignored-predicate findings and the code_path is correctly kept at routes_admin.py:19, the only place where the header value actually decides the outcome (the other three discard it), so the title's "all four modules" framing is scoped down rather than the finding killed.

Production viability (CONDITIONAL_VIABLE): All four route modules do derive identity solely from the unauthenticated X-Caller header, but store.py is a dict-backed stand-in whose _ROWS is never populated (so every fetch returns None and 403s today) and no app factory registering the Blueprints is in the tree.
findings.impact: Full authentication bypass on the only endpoint that enforces ownership: GET /notes/<note_id> returns any tenant's admin note to an unauthenticated caller who sends X-Caller: <victim owner_id>. It also means fixing the three vacuous predicates would not restore security, since the identity they would compare against is attacker-declared.
findings.recommendation: Derive caller_id from an authenticated credential the client cannot mint -- validate the partner bearer issued by tokens.issue (with a real SESSION_SECRET) or a signed session -- and pass that server-derived principal into the predicates instead of a request header. Treat X-Caller as untrusted input per THREAT_MODEL.md, which lists 'HTTP headers that assert identity' as UNTRUSTED. If a header must carry identity, it has to arrive from a trusted proxy that strips and re-sets it, and the proxy must be the only network peer.
