findings.title: Public package declares internal dependency @acme/internal-config that consumers resolve from the public registry
findings.evidence:
package.json:15 declares "@acme/internal-config": "^1.0.0" as a runtime dependency of a package that is itself published publicly ("name": "@acme/billing-cli", "private": false, package.json:2-4). The repository's own .npmrc:2 maps that scope inward -- "@acme:registry=https://npm.internal.acme.example/" -- but that mapping is publisher-side configuration only, for two independent reasons: npm never includes .npmrc in a published tarball, and a package's own .npmrc does not govern how a consumer's npm resolves that package's dependency graph; the consumer's own configuration does. A consumer who has no @acme:registry mapping therefore resolves @acme/internal-config from the default registry at .npmrc:1, https://registry.npmjs.org/. The attacker-controlled input is a package published under the @acme scope on the public registry -- claimable by anyone if acme has not reserved the scope -- and the range "^1.0.0" accepts any 1.x, so a squatted 1.99.0 satisfies it. Its install scripts and module code then execute on the consumer's machine. The internal name is also an intelligence leak in its own right: 'internal-config' tells the squatter exactly what configuration the caller will hand to the module it just took over.

Independent validation: package.json:15 declares "@acme/internal-config": "^1.0.0" in a package published publicly (package.json:4 "private": false). This repo's .npmrc:2 maps @acme to npm.internal.acme.example, but an installing consumer never applies a dependency's own .npmrc - resolution uses the CONSUMER's configuration, which defaults to the public registry named at .npmrc:1 - so downstream the internal name is looked up on registry.npmjs.org. Rule 13, naming the untrusted writer as instructed: any npm account that registers @acme/internal-config (or claims the @acme scope) on the public registry, whose install scripts then execute in every consumer's install; nothing in the tree evidences that Acme owns that scope publicly. Classic dependency confusion.

Production viability (VIABLE): The package is published (private:false) and declares @acme/internal-config; the publisher-side @acme mapping in .npmrc never reaches a consumer, so a consumer without that mapping resolves the internal name from the public registry.
findings.impact: Classic dependency confusion: an attacker who publishes @acme/internal-config publicly gets code execution at install time on every machine that installs @acme/billing-cli without acme's internal registry mapping, and receives whatever internal configuration the CLI passes into the module. A build server that partially resolves from the public registry hands the attacker the same foothold next to the publish credentials.
findings.recommendation: A publicly published package must not depend on an internal-only name: inline or vendor the configuration, or publish a genuine public counterpart. Defensively reserve the @acme scope on registry.npmjs.org so the name can never be answered publicly, and publish a placeholder @acme/internal-config there. Commit a package-lock.json so the resolved registry URL and integrity hash of every dependency are pinned rather than re-resolved from the consumer's registry order, and pin an exact version instead of the ^1.0.0 range. The digest-pinning discipline already used in scripts/fetch-schema.js:18-20 is the same contract applied to fetched artifacts.

findings.title: package.json depends on the typosquat name 'lodahs' resolved from the public registry
findings.evidence:
package.json:16 declares "lodahs": "1.0.1" in "dependencies". 'lodahs' is a character transposition of 'lodash' -- the h and the s are swapped -- and it carries no scope, so it is resolved from the default registry configured at .npmrc:1, "registry=https://registry.npmjs.org/". The untrusted input is therefore the entire published contents of whatever public package answers to that name: its install/postinstall lifecycle scripts and its module body. That content lands on disk and executes during 'npm install' of this package, on every consumer machine and in this repository's own CI. The surrounding entries make the intent clear: chalk, node-fetch and left-pad are real upstream projects and typescript is exact-pinned, so 'lodahs' is the only dependency whose name does not correspond to a real project. The risk does not depend on the name being squatted today -- either an attacker already owns it, or it is an unclaimed public name that any attacker can register and immediately gain install-time execution on everyone who installs @acme/billing-cli ("private": false, package.json:4). There is no lockfile in the tree to pin a resolved tarball and integrity hash, so nothing constrains what the name resolves to.

Independent validation: package.json:16 declares "lodahs": "1.0.1" - one transposition from lodash and, crucially, an UNSCOPED name, so the @acme mapping in .npmrc:2 does not apply and it resolves from the default registry at .npmrc:1 (registry.npmjs.org). Rule 13, naming the untrusted writer as instructed: whoever holds publish rights to the public-registry name `lodahs` - an arbitrary third-party npm account, not Acme - and whose tarball's install lifecycle scripts execute on every `npm ci` in CI and on every developer machine. The exact version pin prevents silent upgrades but does nothing about the first resolution.

Production viability (VIABLE): The unscoped 'lodahs' entry in dependencies resolves from the default public registry configured at .npmrc:1 on every install of this shipped manifest.
findings.impact: Arbitrary code execution at install time on every consumer of the published package, under the consumer's user account -- and inside the release pipeline, in the same process tree as the npm publish token, which lets the attacker publish their own versions of @acme/billing-cli and reach every downstream consumer.
findings.recommendation: Remove the entry; if lodash is actually wanted, declare "lodash" with an exact version. Commit a package-lock.json so every dependency carries a resolved URL and an integrity hash, run installs with 'npm ci --ignore-scripts' in CI, and add a name-similarity check (or an allowlist of approved package names) to the release gate. The exact-pinned entries "node-fetch": "2.7.0" and "typescript": "5.4.5" in this same file are the intended pinning discipline.

findings.title: log_request writes the caller's email and national_id into every request log line
findings.evidence:
app/logging_setup.py emits the caller's direct identifiers at INFO on every request. The decisive line is analytics-service/app/logging_setup.py:12 -- `path, user["id"], user["email"], user["national_id"])` -- whose values are the account holder's registration data resolved from the session and rendered into the format string declared on line 11. The redaction in this module does not save it: `RedactingFormatter` (line 20) is defined but never attached to any handler anywhere in the service, so it applies only if some caller outside this file happens to install it, and its pattern at line 6, `(email|national_id|phone)=([^\s]+)`, matches only the literal `field=value` shape -- a dict repr, a JSON body, or a support-note string carrying the same data passes through untouched. The hardened twin at line 15, `log_request_redacted`, records `path` and the opaque `user["id"]` only, which is the identifier the support use case in the docstring actually needs.

Independent validation: logging_setup.py:11-12 writes user['email'] and user['national_id'] into every request log line, while the sibling log_request_redacted (lines 15-17) logs only the opaque id. Rule 09 checked pragmatically: RedactingFormatter (lines 20-25) would mask exactly these fields, but a tree-wide grep for setFormatter/addHandler/basicConfig returns no hit anywhere in CODE_ROOT, so it is attached to no handler and mitigates nothing on this path. Sensitive identifiers landing in a widely-readable, lower-trust store is CWE-532; MEDIUM stands.

Production viability (VIABLE): log_request writes email and national_id at INFO on every request, and RedactingFormatter is defined but attached to no handler anywhere in the service, so nothing in a standard build strips them.
findings.impact: National ID numbers and email addresses accumulate in plaintext application logs and in whatever aggregation, SIEM or third-party log vendor the handlers forward to -- an audience far wider than the tenant who owns the record, and one that is authenticated at a completely different level. Logs are not in jobs/lifecycle.py's STORES tuple, so this copy of the PII is never covered by the retention purge and survives account deletion indefinitely.
findings.recommendation: Replace the call sites of log_request with the hardened twin log_request_redacted (analytics-service/app/logging_setup.py:15), which logs only the opaque user id. Keep RedactingFormatter but wire it onto every handler at start-up as a backstop rather than as the control, and widen it beyond the `field=value` shape so structured payloads are covered too.

findings.title: handlers.Upload passes the raw ?name query parameter straight to store() as the object key, letting an unauthenticated caller choose the storage path
findings.evidence:
The decisive line is handlers/handlers.go:15: `if err := store(r.URL.Query().Get("name"), body); err != nil {`. `name` is a raw query parameter on /v1/upload, a route that router/routes.go:11 documents as reachable without a session, and it is handed to the storage layer verbatim - there is no length bound, no character allowlist, no rejection of `..` segments, of a leading `/`, or of the empty string, and no server-side prefix binding the key to the caller. The storage layer itself is a stand-in here, but the key string that this caller builds is the attacker-shaped value, and config/env.go:18-21 shows what it is fed to: a `Storage` struct holding a `Bucket` name and a `MaxObjectMB` cap, i.e. a keyed object store whose paths are composed from this string. A name such as `?name=../../../config/keys.json` escapes whatever prefix the store joins the key onto, and any name at all overwrites an existing object, because nothing at handlers.go:9-19 authenticates the caller or namespaces the key. The contrast with the sibling handler on the same public mux is the intended contract: Delivery refuses to act until it checks a signature over the body - `if !verify(r.Header.Get("X-Signature"), body)` at handlers/handlers.go:29, returning 401 at handlers.go:30 - whereas Upload verifies nothing about who is calling or what they name the object.

Independent validation: handlers/handlers.go:15 hands r.URL.Query().Get("name") to store() verbatim as the object key - no length bound, no allowlist, no path.Clean, no empty-string rejection and no server-chosen per-caller prefix - on a route the router documents as reachable without a session (router/routes.go:10-11, registered at :17), and Upload authenticates nobody (handlers.go:9-19). Rule 13 ingress: the ?name query parameter at handlers.go:15. Correction to the finder's IMPACT rather than its status: store() is not defined anywhere in gateway-limits (neither is verify()), so the '../../../config/keys.json escapes the prefix / arbitrary file write' outcome is not demonstrable from this tree; what IS proven at line 15 is an unauthenticated caller choosing and overwriting an arbitrary object key, which supports MEDIUM and no more.

Production viability (CONDITIONAL_VIABLE): handlers.Upload is genuinely wired unauthenticated at router/routes.go:17 through server.go, but store() is not in this tree, so whether the attacker-chosen key escapes the bucket prefix depends on the real storage layer that stands in here.
findings.impact: Unauthenticated creation and overwrite of arbitrary objects in the gateway's bucket, including other tenants' objects; against a filesystem-backed or path-joining store, writes land outside the intended prefix (configuration or credential files), turning an open upload endpoint into arbitrary file write.
findings.recommendation: Validate the key before it leaves the handler: reject empty, cap the length, allowlist [A-Za-z0-9._-], apply path.Clean and assert strings.HasPrefix against a server-chosen per-caller prefix - or ignore the client-supplied name entirely and mint a server-side UUID key. Gate the write on caller identity the way the hardened sibling Delivery gates on its signature check at handlers/handlers.go:29-32.

findings.title: middleware.Throttle keys its bucket on r.RemoteAddr, whose ephemeral port the attacker controls, so a fresh TCP connection resets the burst and every connection leaks a map entry
findings.class: Rate limit bypass via attacker-controlled key
findings.evidence:
The decisive line is middleware/limits.go:20: `if !allow(r.RemoteAddr, config.RateLimitBurst) {`. Go populates `r.RemoteAddr` with the connection's `host:port`, and the port is the client's ephemeral source port - chosen by the attacker's own kernel and freely settable by the attacker. The bucket key is therefore per-connection, not per-client. In `allow` (middleware/limits.go:28-38) an unseen key takes the `!ok` branch at limits.go:29-32 and is seeded with a full fresh `burst` (config.RateLimitBurst, default 20, config/env.go:35), so a caller who opens a new TCP connection every 20 requests never reaches the `bucket <= 0` rejection at limits.go:33 and is never throttled. The untrusted input is the source port of each connection from an A1 caller, and it lands directly as the map key at limits.go:29 and limits.go:36. The same attacker-controlled key has a second effect at limits.go:36: every distinct key is inserted into `buckets` and nothing in the file ever deletes, expires or bounds that map, so it grows by one entry per connection for the lifetime of the process - unbounded, attacker-driven memory growth inside the component whose job is to bound consumption.

Independent validation: middleware/limits.go:20 keys the bucket on r.RemoteAddr, which net/http fills with host:PORT of the accepted connection, so every new TCP connection from the same client misses the map at line 29 and is handed a fresh `burst` - the throttle this module exists to enforce is bypassed by reconnecting, and the entry written at line 36 is never deleted or refilled (map at line 40). Rule 07 side: ENFORCEMENT side, not hardening - Throttle's own doc comment (line 17) states the cap it is meant to apply and config.RateLimitBurst (env.go:35) declares it, so per the brief's gateway-limits carve-out an unenforced declared cap is a real defect. Rule 13 ingress: the client-chosen source port in r.RemoteAddr at line 20. Caveat: router/routes.go:15-17 wires only BodyLimit, so Throttle's caller is the unshown router/private.go referenced at routes.go:11 - the flaw is intrinsic to the exported middleware (rule 08).

Production viability (CONDITIONAL_VIABLE): The per-connection bucket key is a real defect in the shipped middleware, but middleware.Throttle is exported and wired into no route in this tree (router/routes.go registers only BodyLimit; the authenticated mux router/private.go is absent), so viability is conditional on the private router that mounts it.
findings.impact: The burst ceiling is bypassed for free - one extra TCP handshake buys a full new quota - so no route protected by Throttle is meaningfully rate limited against a determined caller, while the same traffic inflates the buckets map without limit until the gateway exhausts memory.
findings.recommendation: Key on client identity rather than the connection: strip the port with net.SplitHostPort(r.RemoteAddr) and, when the gateway sits behind a proxy, take the client address from an operator-configured trusted forwarded hop rather than the raw header. Back it with a real token bucket that refills over time and evicts idle keys - note that `allow` today only ever decrements and never replenishes (middleware/limits.go:28-38), so a key that does stay stable becomes a permanent one-shot quota that never recovers - e.g. a size-capped LRU of golang.org/x/time/rate.Limiter values.

findings.title: fetch-native.js preinstall installs a downloaded binary with no digest or signature verification
findings.evidence:
The untrusted input is the HTTP response body served for 'https://downloads.example.net/billing-native/latest/billing-native' (scripts/fetch-native.js:17) -- a host outside this repository's control, whose bytes are chosen by anyone who compromises that origin/CDN, takes over the downloads.example.net name, or terminates TLS in front of the consumer. main() awaits the transfer at line 19 ("await download(url, dest);") and on the very next line makes the result executable: "execSync(`chmod +x ${dest}`);" (line 20). Nothing between the socket and the executable bit inspects the bytes -- no sha256 comparison, no detached signature, no integrity value, no pinned version, not even a length check. The 'latest' path segment means the publisher cannot pin it either. This script is wired to the lifecycle hook: package.json:8 declares "preinstall": "node scripts/fetch-native.js", so it runs on every consumer 'npm install' of the published package ("private": false, package.json:4) without the consumer ever invoking it. The digest-pinned sibling in the same directory shows the intended contract: scripts/fetch-schema.js buffers the whole body, computes crypto.createHash('sha256') (fetch-schema.js:17) and throws 'schema digest mismatch, refusing to build' (fetch-schema.js:18-20) when it does not equal PINNED_SHA256 (fetch-schema.js:5). fetch-native.js is the unpinned member of that pair, and it is the one that both runs at install time and produces an executable rather than a JSON file. Transport itself is sound -- https.get with default options keeps certificate validation on -- so the gap is integrity, not TLS.

Independent validation: scripts/fetch-native.js:19 awaits the body of https://downloads.example.net/billing-native/latest/billing-native (line 17) and line 20 immediately makes it executable, with no digest comparison, signature check or immutable version pin anywhere in the file - and package.json:8 wires it to `preinstall`, so it runs on every consumer install. Rule 13 writer: whoever serves that mutable `latest` path - the download host/CDN operator or anyone who compromises or takes over that origin; HTTPS authenticates the host but says nothing about artifact integrity. The digest-pinned sibling scripts/fetch-schema.js:5,17-20 is the repo's own fail-closed contract, which this script does not follow, so this is an intrinsic CWE-494 integrity gap, not a hygiene wish.

Production viability (VIABLE): The preinstall hook downloads from a third-party host and chmod +x's the result with no digest, signature or version pin; the sibling fetch-schema.js verifies a PINNED_SHA256, proving the control was available and omitted here.
findings.impact: Whoever controls the download response gets arbitrary code execution on every machine that installs @acme/billing-cli: developer laptops and CI runners alike. Because the destination is made executable and placed on the system PATH, the payload persists and runs again later. On the release pipeline the same install runs in the process tree that holds the npm publish token, converting a single CDN or DNS compromise into ownership of the package itself and of every downstream consumer.
findings.recommendation: Apply the pattern of the hardened twin scripts/fetch-schema.js verbatim: buffer the response, compute sha256 over the bytes, compare against a constant pinned in source (PINNED_SHA256, fetch-schema.js:5) and throw before anything touches the filesystem -- and additionally verify a publisher signature (minisign/cosign) since a binary is higher-value than a schema. Pin an immutable version in the URL instead of 'latest'. Better still, remove the preinstall hook entirely and ship the platform binary as an optionalDependency per-platform package, so npm's own integrity hash and lockfile cover it.

findings.title: aws_iam_role_policy.worker grants Action "*" on Resource "*" to the EC2 worker role
findings.evidence:
The inline policy attached to the `worker` role is unbounded: `Action = "*"` (line 49) and `Resource = "*"` (line 50), with no `Condition` block. The role is assumable by the EC2 service (`identifiers = ["ec2.amazonaws.com"]`, line 95), so its credentials are vended by the instance metadata service to anything running on -- or able to make the instance make a request on its behalf -- the worker hosts. The attacker-controlled input is any request that reaches an application on a worker instance and can be steered at `http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/iam/security-credentials/worker` (a server-side request forgery in the worker application, or any command execution foothold on the box, including one obtained through the CI path in .github/workflows/deploy.yml). Those credentials land against the policy on line 49, which authorises every action in the account. The hardened twin sits directly below it: `aws_iam_role_policy.deployer` (lines 55-67) enumerates exactly two actions (`s3:PutObject`, `s3:GetObject`), scopes them to one resource ARN (`${aws_s3_bucket.reports.arn}/*`), and adds a `Condition` on `aws:ResourceAccount` pinned to `var.account_id` -- the file therefore already states what a correctly-scoped role in this platform looks like.

Independent validation: main.tf:45-52 renders an inline policy with Action = "*" (line 49) on Resource = "*" (line 50) attached to aws_iam_role.worker (line 44), whose trust policy admits ec2.amazonaws.com (main.tf:90-97): anything that reaches that instance's IMDS credentials holds account-wide administrator. Intrinsic misconfiguration in the resource's own logic, no untrusted input required. Rule 10: stripped main.tf:55 from code_paths - aws_iam_role_policy.deployer is the least-privilege sibling (two scoped actions plus an aws:ResourceAccount condition) and is not part of the flawed block.

Production viability (VIABLE): The inline policy grants Action '*' on Resource '*' with no condition to a role assumable by EC2, which is the infrastructure state this Terraform applies; the deployer role in the same file shows the scoped form was available.
findings.impact: Any foothold on a worker instance escalates to full administrative control of the AWS account: read and exfiltrate the billing reports bucket, snapshot and share the billing RDS instance, create and attach IAM users and access keys for durable persistence, rewrite the CloudFront-fronted marketing site, and delete or ransom every resource in the account.
findings.recommendation: Replace the wildcard with the enumerated actions the worker actually performs and the exact resource ARNs it touches, following the least-privilege sibling `aws_iam_role_policy.deployer` in the same file (lines 55-67), including its `Condition = { StringEquals = { "aws:ResourceAccount" = var.account_id } }` guard. Require IMDSv2 on the worker instances (`metadata_options { http_tokens = "required" }`) so an SSRF cannot read the credentials with a plain GET, and add an IAM permissions boundary to the role so no future policy can widen it back to `*`.

findings.title: aws_db_instance.billing stores the billing database unencrypted (storage_encrypted = false)
findings.evidence:
The Postgres instance holding billing data is created with encryption at rest explicitly disabled: `storage_encrypted = false` (line 76). Beyond the raw volume, this setting governs what can be done with the instance's snapshots: an UNENCRYPTED RDS snapshot may be shared with arbitrary AWS accounts, and may be marked public, whereas an encrypted snapshot cannot be made public at all and cross-account sharing additionally requires an explicit grant on the KMS key. The concrete attacker action is therefore `rds:CreateDBSnapshot` on `billing-${var.env}` followed by `rds:ModifyDBSnapshotAttribute --attribute restore --values-to-add all`, which any holder of the `worker` role credentials can issue because that role's inline policy is `Action = "*"` on `Resource = "*"` (line 49). Line 76 is what makes that second call succeed and turns a snapshot into a portable copy of the database that leaves the account with no KMS key to stop it. The same resource passes the password in as a `sensitive` variable (lines 75, 103-106), so the file is not careless as a whole -- the encryption flag was set to false deliberately.

Independent validation: main.tf:76 sets storage_encrypted = false on the Postgres instance holding billing data (main.tf:69-78), an explicit opt-out of encryption at rest (CWE-311) that RDS cannot apply retroactively - the instance must be recreated from a snapshot to fix it, so the defect is baked in at create time. This is a missing data-protection control on the storage itself rather than a wrapper-level hardening wish; MEDIUM is right because exploitation needs access to snapshots or the underlying media rather than a remote trigger.

Production viability (VIABLE): storage_encrypted = false is the applied state of the billing database, and it is what makes the snapshot of it shareable cross-account or public, which an encrypted snapshot could not be.
findings.impact: A single compromised in-account credential converts into an offline, restorable copy of the entire billing database -- customer PII, billing records, and any tokens stored in it -- in an AWS account the attacker controls, with no key material required and no further access to the running instance. Physical and AWS-internal media exposure paths are also left uncovered.
findings.recommendation: Set `storage_encrypted = true` and supply a customer-managed `kms_key_id` so snapshot sharing requires an explicit key grant that can be audited and revoked; encryption at rest cannot be enabled in place, so the change is a snapshot-encrypt-restore migration. Pair it with the scoped-credential discipline the file already applies to `aws_iam_role_policy.deployer` (lines 55-67) so no role holds blanket `rds:*` in the first place.

findings.title: download() in fetch-native.js reports success on stream finish without checking res.statusCode
findings.evidence:
The untrusted input is the status line and the completeness of the response from downloads.example.net (scripts/fetch-native.js:17). Inside download() the response callback's first statement opens the destination -- "const file = fs.createWriteStream(dest);" (line 9) -- which truncates any existing /usr/local/bin/billing-native before a single byte has been examined. It then pipes whatever came back (line 10) and declares success at the decisive line 11: "file.on('finish', () => resolve(dest));". res.statusCode is never read anywhere in the file, and https.get does not follow redirects, so a 301/302 body, a 404 HTML error page, a 500, or a captive-portal interstitial is written verbatim to the destination and reported to main() as a completed download, which then chmod +x's it (line 20). The error wiring is equally partial: the only handler is ".on('error', reject)" attached to the ClientRequest at line 12 -- there is no res.on('error') and no file.on('error'), so a mid-stream socket abort or a write failure (EACCES when npm is not run as root, ENOSPC) emits 'error' on a stream with no listener, and a premature close still leaves a truncated file in place. main() at line 23 is called with no .catch(). The sibling scripts/fetch-schema.js does not need a status check to be safe because its digest comparison rejects any body that is not the expected artifact -- fetch-native.js has neither guard.

Independent validation: In download() (scripts/fetch-native.js:6-14) the destination is opened and truncated at line 9 before anything inspects the response, and line 11 resolves the promise on the write stream's 'finish' event; res.statusCode is never read anywhere in the file and https.get does not follow redirects, so a 30x/404/500 body is written over /usr/local/bin/billing-native and reported to main() as success, which then chmod +x's it (line 20). The only error handler is on the ClientRequest (line 12) - none on res or on the file stream - so a truncated transfer also leaves a partial file and still resolves. That is a concrete misuse of the API inside the function's own logic, not a lint nit; rule 13 writer: the download host, which chooses the status line and body.

Production viability (VIABLE): res.statusCode is never read anywhere in the file and the destination stream is opened before any byte is examined, so any non-200 body or truncated transfer is written verbatim and reported as success on every install.
findings.impact: An attacker who can make the download host return any non-200 response -- or an on-path device that injects an error page -- replaces the previously installed billing-native with content of their choosing, which is then marked executable on the system PATH; the install reports success. Even without an attacker, a transient 502 or a truncated transfer silently destroys a working binary and installs a partial file, so any process that later invokes billing-native by name executes attacker-supplied or corrupt content.
findings.recommendation: Reject unless res.statusCode === 200 before creating the write stream; download to a temporary file in the same directory and rename into place only after the status check and the digest check succeed, so a failed fetch never destroys the existing artifact. Attach 'error' handlers to both res and the write stream and reject the promise from them, unlink the partial file on failure, and give main() a .catch() that exits non-zero. scripts/fetch-schema.js:18-20 is the fail-closed model to copy.

findings.title: fetch-native.js preinstall writes its downloaded executable into system-wide /usr/local/bin
findings.class: Install script writes outside package sandbox
findings.evidence:
The destination is hard-coded at scripts/fetch-native.js:18: "const dest = '/usr/local/bin/billing-native';", and the untrusted content written there is the unverified remote body from line 17, delivered by the preinstall hook (package.json:8) on every consumer install. This is a defect independent of whether the bytes are verified: a package lifecycle script is writing an executable outside its own package directory, into a directory that is on the default PATH of every user of the host. Three consequences follow from this line alone. (1) The write only succeeds when npm runs as root or as an admin who owns /usr/local/bin, so the script's design pressures consumers into 'sudo npm install', which means every other weakness in this file -- the unverified body, the unchecked status, the shell call at line 20 -- executes with root privilege. (2) npm has no record of a file it did not place under node_modules, so 'npm uninstall @acme/billing-cli' leaves the executable on the machine permanently, outliving the package that installed it. (3) The artifact is machine-global rather than project-local: any process, any user, any other project that runs 'billing-native' by name resolves this file. The repository already contains the correct, package-local location for exactly this artifact -- vendor/billing-native -- which nothing in the fetch path uses.

Independent validation: scripts/fetch-native.js:18 hard-codes dest = '/usr/local/bin/billing-native' and line 20 marks it executable, driven by the preinstall hook declared at package.json:8, which fires on every install of this publicly published package (package.json:4 "private": false). A lifecycle script writing an executable outside its own package directory onto the system-wide PATH is an affirmative unsafe-install-location defect - npm neither tracks nor removes the file on uninstall, and the choice pressures consumers into `sudo npm install`, running everything else in this script as root. Rule 13 writer: the remote body fetched at line 17, which nothing in the file verifies.

Production viability (VIABLE): package.json:8 declares the preinstall hook, so every consumer install of this published package (private:false) runs a script that writes an executable to the system-wide /usr/local/bin - the shipped manifest is the deployed state.
findings.impact: The blast radius of the install script expands from one project's node_modules to the whole host and to every user on it, with root-owned persistence that survives uninstalling the package. An attacker who lands content through the fetch path (see the unverified-download finding) obtains a permanent, PATH-resolvable, root-installed executable rather than a removable file inside a project directory.
findings.recommendation: Write to a path derived from __dirname inside the package (path.join(__dirname, '..', 'vendor', 'billing-native') -- the location vendor/billing-native already establishes) and expose it through the package's "bin" map so npm owns placement and removal; never require root for an install. Set the executable bit with fs.chmodSync(dest, 0o755) instead of shelling out through execSync at line 20. The sibling scripts/fetch-schema.js writes 'schema.json' relative to the working directory rather than into a system directory, and is not wired to a lifecycle hook at all.

findings.title: write_token() persists the publishing token in world-readable /tmp/packer-cache/token
findings.evidence:
write_token() stores the credential that authorizes publishing to the mirror. Line 61 pins the destination to `path = CACHE / "token"` -- i.e. the fixed, world-traversable `/tmp/packer-cache/token` from the constant at line 12 -- line 62 does `CACHE.mkdir(exist_ok=True)`, and line 63 writes the secret with `path.write_text(token)`. `Path.write_text` opens with the default mode 0o666 masked by the process umask, which under the documented sudo invocation is typically 022, leaving the token file mode 0644: readable by every account on the host, including A6, the unprivileged local user in the threat model. Nothing narrows this -- no `os.open` with an explicit mode, no `os.chmod`, no `os.umask`, no attempt to place the file outside a shared directory. The token is also written in cleartext and left behind between runs (the docstring says 'Remembers the publishing token between runs'), so the exposure window is not the duration of a build but indefinite. The same `exist_ok=True` on line 62 accepts a /tmp/packer-cache that A6 pre-created and owns, and `write_text` follows symlinks, so the token can additionally be redirected into a file the attacker already reads. The hardened twin is directly below: write_token_privately() at lines 69-74 puts the token under `Path.home()/".config"/"packer"`, creates that directory with `mode=0o700`, and writes the file through `os.open(path, os.O_WRONLY|os.O_CREAT|os.O_TRUNC, 0o600)` so the permissions are set at creation time rather than after the secret is already on disk.

Independent validation: packer.py:61-63 writes the publishing token with path.write_text into /tmp/packer-cache/token, in a directory created by mkdir(exist_ok=True) with no mode argument, so the file lands with the default 0o666 & ~umask (typically 0644) in a shared directory; the sibling write_token_privately (lines 67-75) uses ~/.config/packer with mode 0o700 and os.open(..., 0o600). Ingress (rule 13): any local user on the host can read it, and the README documents this tool's publish path running under sudo, so a root-written token is exposed to unprivileged readers. HIGH stands. Refined code_paths per rule 10: dropped the CACHE constant at line 12.

Production viability (CONDITIONAL_VIABLE): write_text() leaving the publishing token at umask-default 0644 in /tmp/packer-cache is real, but no command in main() reaches write_token(), and the resulting mode depends on the inherited umask (0022 under the documented sudo invocation).
findings.impact: Any unprivileged local account on the host reads the publishing token straight out of /tmp and can publish arbitrary bundles to the internal mirror under the release identity -- a supply-chain compromise of every downstream consumer of that mirror. THREAT_MODEL lists the publish token as a first-class asset. The persistence between runs means a low-privilege foothold obtained at any time captures the credential.
findings.recommendation: Use the hardened twin already present in this file: write_token_privately() (packer.py:67-75), which writes to `~/.config/packer/token` with a 0o700 directory and an `os.open(..., 0o600)` file so the mode is applied atomically at creation. Delete write_token() and its /tmp destination. Add `os.O_NOFOLLOW` to that open, and prefer the platform keyring or an environment-supplied token over on-disk persistence; if a file must be used under sudo, write it as the invoking user, not as root, and clear it when the publish completes.

findings.title: store.expired compares created_at against itself, so the retention predicate can never return True
findings.evidence:
store.py:17 declares the retention predicate and store.py:18 is its entire body: `return isoparse(created_at) + timedelta(days=RETENTION_DAYS) < isoparse(created_at)`. Both sides of the comparison parse the same created_at string; the left side is the right side plus a positive RETENTION_DAYS (90 by default, settings.py:9, and "90" in docker-compose.yml:7). A value strictly greater than another value is never less than it, so the expression is constant False for every possible input -- no created_at a caller can supply, however old or however malformed-but-parseable, makes it fire. The untrusted input is the created_at timestamp carried on any stored intake record submitted through the portal; it lands at store.py:18 and is discarded into a comparison whose result is fixed. The right-hand operand is plainly meant to be the current time -- the reference point against which an age is measured -- so the defect is a self-comparison where `datetime.now(timezone.utc)` belongs.

Independent validation: store.py:18 reads isoparse(created_at) + timedelta(days=RETENTION_DAYS) < isoparse(created_at): both sides derive from the same created_at, so with RETENTION_DAYS = 90 (settings.py:9, echoed at docker-compose.yml:7 and .env.example:3) the predicate is unconditionally False and expired() can never return True. The right-hand side should be the current time. Deterministic intrinsic logic defect (rule 08): the declared 90-day retention bound is never enforced, so submitted records are retained indefinitely. Not a data-flow finding, so rule 13 does not apply.

Production viability (CONDITIONAL_VIABLE): The predicate is tautologically False for every input, which no configuration can change, but expired() has no in-tree caller and the retention job that would act on it is absent from this slice.
findings.impact: The 90-day retention window is never enforced: no intake record, note, export or partner row is ever classified as expired, so customer PII (national_id, email, support notes, risk score) accumulates indefinitely in violation of the service's own declared policy. Every day of non-deletion enlarges the pool of records exposed by the unauthenticated read endpoints in this same package.
findings.recommendation: Compare against the present, not against the record: `return isoparse(created_at) + timedelta(days=RETENTION_DAYS) < datetime.now(timezone.utc)`, importing datetime/timezone alongside the existing timedelta import at store.py:3, and handle naive-vs-aware timestamps explicitly. Add a test that pins a created_at 91 days in the past and asserts expired() is True -- the current implementation cannot pass it, which is exactly why the bug survived.

findings.title: Unescaped customer note interpolated into HTML in invoiceNote yields stored XSS
findings.evidence:
lib/render.js:4 builds the note block of the rendered invoice and line 5 interpolates the argument raw into markup: ``return `
${note}
`;``. The comment above it names the source of that argument -- 'Free-text note the customer typed on the invoice' (line 3) -- so the value is attacker-controlled text stored on the invoice and later rendered into a viewer's browser, which is THREAT_MODEL profile A3 ('controls a customer ticket, an invoice note ... their text reaches an LLM, a browser, or a log'). Nothing between the store and line 5 encodes it. The hardened twin is the next function in the same module: `customerName` at lib/render.js:9 renders an equally untrusted field through the imported encoder -- ``return `${escapeHtml(name)}`;`` (line 10) -- and `footer` at line 15 coerces its argument with `Number(year)`. `escape-html` is a declared dependency (package.json:10) and is already required at lib/render.js:1, so the encoder was in hand and simply not applied to the one field an outsider writes. A note of `` is emitted as live markup on the invoice page. Independent validation: lib/render.js:5 interpolates `note` straight into an HTML string with no escaping, while the sibling customerName at render.js:10 wraps the same class of value in escapeHtml(name) and footer at render.js:15 coerces with Number(year) - so the intended contract is explicit in-file and invoiceNote is the deviation, with escape-html already a declared dependency (package.json:10). Raw interpolation into HTML is a direct injection path in the function's own logic, so rule 08 keeps it valid despite no in-tree caller; the parameter's provenance is declared in-file at render.js:3 ('Free-text note the customer typed on the invoice'). MEDIUM is correct, since no route in this excerpt renders the output. Production viability (CONDITIONAL_VIABLE): The raw interpolation of the customer note into markup is unconditional in lib/render.js:5, but the module has no in-tree caller and the template/response path that would deliver it to a browser is absent from this slice.
findings.impact: Stored cross-site scripting in the invoice view. Script written by the party who submitted the invoice runs in the session of whoever opens it -- typically the billing operator -- and can read the page, exfiltrate the session token or the invoice data, and drive the authenticated billing endpoints (including the refund capability listed as an asset in THREAT_MODEL) as that operator.
findings.recommendation:
Encode the note the way the hardened twin `customerName` (lib/render.js:9-11) already encodes its field: ``return `
${escapeHtml(note)}
`;`` using the `escape-html` import already present at lib/render.js:1. If the note is meant to carry formatting, run it through a sanitiser with an explicit tag/attribute allowlist rather than raw interpolation, and add a Content-Security-Policy without unsafe-inline as defence in depth.

findings.title: delete_account marks only the customers row, so deleted accounts are never purged from events, exports, search_index or backups
findings.evidence:
jobs/lifecycle.py splits deletion from retention in a way that leaves four of five stores unreachable. The input is the `account_id` an account holder submits with a close/erasure request. The decisive line is analytics-service/jobs/lifecycle.py:10 -- `db.execute("UPDATE customers SET deleted_at = now() WHERE id = %s", [account_id])` -- a single-table write. Its counterpart, `purge_expired` (line 13), iterates `for store in STORES` (line 16) over `STORES = ("customers", "events", "exports", "search_index", "backups")` (line 5) and deletes with `WHERE deleted_at IS NOT NULL AND deleted_at < %s` (line 17), i.e. it depends on each store carrying its own `deleted_at` marker. Nothing in the service ever sets that marker outside `customers`, so on the other four stores the predicate can never match and the purge is a no-op that reads, to anyone auditing the code, as full coverage. There is no hardened twin here: the pair is internally inconsistent, and the STORES tuple is the written statement of the contract the deletion path fails to meet.

Independent validation: lifecycle.py:10 updates only the customers table, yet the module itself declares five stores at line 5 and purge_expired (lines 13-17) sweeps all five gated on a deleted_at that nothing in the tree ever sets outside customers -- so within this module's own lifecycle logic the deletion mark never propagates. That is a real retention/erasure defect, but no data crosses to a lower-trust holder and no attacker is involved: it is data remanence inside the same trust boundary, so I lowered the finder's MEDIUM to LOW.

Production viability (VIABLE): delete_account writes deleted_at only on customers while purge_expired sweeps five stores on that marker, so four of the five can never be purged - a defect complete in the shipped job with no configuration involved.
findings.impact: PII of users who asked to be deleted -- event history, exported reports, indexed names and emails, and backup copies carrying national_id and support notes -- is retained indefinitely while both the user and any auditor reading purge_expired believe it was erased after the 30-day window. Every later exposure of one of those stores discloses data the service already reported as deleted: an unauthenticated read of an export or backup bucket (threat-model actor A7 probing public storage), or the search index simply answering a query for the deleted person's name.
findings.recommendation: Make delete_account fan the tombstone out to every name in STORES inside one transaction (or write a single deletion ledger that purge_expired joins against per store) so the two functions are driven by the same list. Add an assertion/test that the set of stores delete_account writes equals STORES, so adding a store to the tuple cannot silently create another unreachable copy.

findings.title: stage() creates predictable staging files inside the shared, pre-creatable /tmp/packer-cache directory
findings.evidence:
CACHE is the hardcoded constant `Path("/tmp/packer-cache")` at line 12 -- a fixed path in the world-writable, world-traversable /tmp. stage() then does `CACHE.mkdir(exist_ok=True)` at line 29 and builds `path = CACHE / f"stage-{os.getpid()}-{name}"` at line 30, writing through it with `path.write_bytes(b"")` at line 31. Two attacker-controlled preconditions make this exploitable by A6, an unprivileged local user on the same host. First, `exist_ok=True` means that if A6 has already created /tmp/packer-cache (they can: /tmp is world-writable and the name is a compile-time constant, so it can be planted long before any build runs), the mkdir silently succeeds and the privileged process proceeds to write inside a directory whose owner, mode and contents the attacker controls -- the sticky bit on /tmp protects /tmp itself, not the attacker's own subdirectory. Second, the filename carries no secret: it is the literal prefix `stage-`, `os.getpid()` (a small, guessable, brute-forceable integer -- A6 can simply pre-create every candidate) and `name`. So A6 can place a symlink at the exact target path in advance; `path.write_bytes(b"")` at line 31 follows it and truncates whatever it points at, with the privileges of the process -- root, per the README's documented sudo operation. There is no O_EXCL, no O_NOFOLLOW, no mode argument and no ownership check anywhere on this path. The hardened twin is immediately below: stage_privately() at lines 37-38 builds a fresh 0700 directory with `tempfile.mkdtemp(prefix="packer-")` and then allocates the file inside it with `tempfile.mkstemp(...)`, which uses an unguessable name and O_CREAT|O_EXCL|O_NOFOLLOW at mode 0600.

Independent validation: packer.py:29-31 does CACHE.mkdir(exist_ok=True) on the shared path /tmp/packer-cache and then write_bytes to CACHE/f'stage-{os.getpid()}-{name}', a name a local user can predict and pre-create; exist_ok=True silently accepts a directory or symlink an attacker planted first, and neither the directory nor the file is given a restrictive mode. The sibling stage_privately (lines 35-40) uses mkdtemp/mkstemp. Ingress (rule 13): any local unprivileged user on the same host owns the pre-created path. HIGH stands because line 28 states the staged bundle is what gets signed, so controlling it means getting attacker content signed with the release key. Refined code_paths per rule 10: dropped the CACHE constant at line 12.

Production viability (CONDITIONAL_VIABLE): The predictable name in world-writable /tmp with mkdir(exist_ok=True) is exactly what ships, but main() dispatches only `unpack`, so the stage/sign command path that calls it is not wired in this slice and the attack additionally needs the documented privileged invocation on a shared host.
findings.impact: A local unprivileged user pre-creates the cache directory and a symlink at the predictable staging path and has the sudo-run packer truncate an arbitrary root-owned file (/etc/shadow, a service binary, an audit log) -- integrity destruction and denial of service as root. The same attacker-owned directory also lets them read, replace or swap staged bundle content between staging and signing, so a bundle that gets signed need not be the bundle that was staged.
findings.recommendation: Replace stage() with the hardened twin already in this file: stage_privately() (packer.py:35-40), which uses `tempfile.mkdtemp(prefix="packer-")` for a private 0700 directory and `tempfile.mkstemp(...)` inside it, so the name is unguessable and the file is opened with O_EXCL|O_NOFOLLOW at 0600 -- a pre-created path causes a hard failure instead of a followed symlink. If a stable cache location is genuinely required, create it with `os.makedirs(CACHE, mode=0o700, exist_ok=False)` (or verify with os.lstat that it already exists, is a directory, is owned by the running uid and is not group/other-writable), and open every file under it with `os.open(..., os.O_WRONLY|os.O_CREAT|os.O_EXCL|os.O_NOFOLLOW, 0o600)`.

findings.title: sign() passes the bundle path to gpg with no '--' terminator, allowing gpg option injection
findings.evidence:
sign() shells out to gpg at line 45: `subprocess.run(["gpg", "--local-user", key_id, "--detach-sign", path], check=True)`. Neither `key_id` nor `path` is separated from gpg's own options by an end-of-options `--` marker, and `path` is never normalised or resolved before being handed over. gpg parses any argument beginning with `-` as an option regardless of where it sits in the argument vector, so a bundle name that starts with a dash stops being a filename and becomes gpg configuration. The name is attacker-shaped from two directions: it can arrive as the value the operator was handed (a bundle filename chosen by whoever produced the bundle), and it can be manufactured on disk -- unpack() at line 18 extracts unfiltered archive member names into the current working directory (line 92, `unpack(args.value, ".")`), so a tarball member literally named `--output=/etc/cron.d/packer` or `-o/root/.ssh/authorized_keys` materialises as a real relative path in the build directory and is then a plausible bundle argument. Reaching gpg, such a value turns a detach-sign into an arbitrary-file write (`--output`), silences prompts (`--batch --yes`), or redirects trust material (`--homedir`, `--options` to load an attacker-written gpg config file, which itself can set `--output`). Under the README's documented sudo operation the resulting write happens as root. The hardened twin is the very next function: verify() at lines 50-51 does both things sign() omits -- `Path(path).resolve(strict=True)` turns the name into an existing absolute path (so it cannot begin with `-`), and the argument vector is `["gpg", "--verify", "--", str(resolved)]` with an explicit `--` before the operand.

Independent validation: packer.py:45 passes `path` as the trailing positional of ['gpg','--local-user',key_id,'--detach-sign',path] with no '--' terminator, so a path beginning with '-' is parsed by gpg as an option; the sibling verify (line 51) uses '--' plus resolve(strict=True), so the module itself treats the terminator as the control. Rule 13 is UNKNOWN rather than FAIL: sign() has no caller in the tree and I cannot cite an ingress for `path`, so the argument-injection primitive is latent -- it survives on rule 08 as an intrinsic flaw in the function's own argv construction, but I lowered MEDIUM to LOW for the undemonstrated reachability. Refined code_paths per rule 10: dropped line 51 (the correct sibling) and line 18 (a different finding).

Production viability (CONDITIONAL_VIABLE): The missing `--` terminator is a genuine omission next to the hardened verify() twin at packer.py:51, but sign() has no caller in main() and exploitation further requires a bundle path that begins with a dash reaching the operator.
findings.impact: A dash-leading bundle name converts the signing step into attacker-directed gpg behaviour: arbitrary file creation/overwrite through `--output` (as root on the sudo path, e.g. a cron or sudoers drop-in giving local privilege escalation), loading of an attacker-controlled gpg configuration via `--options`, or suppression of confirmation prompts so the operator never sees the substitution. It also lets the signing key be applied to a target the operator did not intend.
findings.recommendation: Mirror the hardened twin verify() (packer.py:48-51) exactly: resolve the operand first with `Path(path).resolve(strict=True)` so it is a real absolute path, then build the vector as `["gpg", "--local-user", key_id, "--detach-sign", "--", str(resolved)]` with the `--` terminator before the file operand. Validate `key_id` against a strict allowlist pattern (hex fingerprint / known key id) rather than passing it through, since it sits in option position too. Additionally reject any candidate bundle name whose basename begins with '-' before it is used at all.

findings.title: publish() resolves the 'uploader' helper through $PATH while documented to run under sudo
findings.evidence:
publish() executes the upload helper by bare program name at line 56: `subprocess.run(["uploader", bundle], check=True)`. `uploader` is not an absolute path, so the kernel/exec machinery resolves it by scanning the inherited `PATH` in order and running the first hit. The README states this tool is 'Documented as running under `sudo` for the `publish` command', which makes the resolution security-relevant: whoever controls any directory that appears in the effective PATH before the real helper controls what root executes. That is squarely A6's position in THREAT_MODEL -- an unprivileged local user on a host where cli-packer runs under sudo. Two concrete routes: (1) the invoking environment's PATH survives into the privileged process whenever sudo is configured with `env_keep += PATH`, `!secure_path`, or is invoked as `sudo -E`, so A6 who can influence the operator's environment prepends a directory holding a file named `uploader`; (2) even with sudo's secure_path intact, secure_path routinely contains `/usr/local/bin`, a directory that is group-writable or attacker-writable on many hosts and that supply-chain.md records as an actual install target on this estate -- A6 drops `uploader` there and it wins over anything later in the list. Nothing in this file pins the binary: there is no absolute path, no `shutil.which` result validated against an allowlist, no ownership/mode check on the resolved file, and no explicit `env=` narrowing what the child inherits. `bundle` is likewise passed with no `--` terminator, so a dash-leading name is additionally parsed as an option by the helper.

Independent validation: packer.py:56 runs subprocess.run(['uploader', bundle], check=True) with a bare program name, so the helper is resolved through $PATH at call time, and the README states this command is documented to run under sudo. Judged against that documented context rather than a hypothetical one, this is CWE-426: a local user able to prepend a directory to the PATH the privileged invocation inherits gets root code execution, and the code carries no mitigation of its own -- no absolute path, no env scrub. Ingress (rule 13): PATH is attacker-influenced environment, not internal state. HIGH stands.

Production viability (CONDITIONAL_VIABLE): Resolving `uploader` by bare name is what ships, and the README states the tool is documented as running under sudo, but publish() is not dispatched by main() and the escalation depends on an inherited PATH that sudo's secure_path would otherwise sanitise.
findings.impact: A local unprivileged user who can write into any directory that precedes the genuine helper on the privileged process's PATH gets arbitrary code execution as root the next time an operator runs the documented `sudo packer publish` -- a straight local privilege escalation to host root, which THREAT_MODEL lists as an asset ('host root on the sudo path'). The same planted binary is also handed the bundle being published and runs inside the process that holds the publishing credential.
findings.recommendation: Invoke the helper by a pinned absolute path (e.g. `/usr/lib/packer/uploader`) resolved from a trusted, non-user-writable install location, and before exec verify with `os.stat` that the resolved file is owned by root and is not group- or other-writable; abort otherwise. Pass an explicit `env={"PATH": "/usr/bin:/bin", ...}` to subprocess.run so nothing about the caller's environment reaches the privileged child, and add the end-of-options `--` before `bundle` the way the hardened verify() (packer.py:51) does for its operand. Better still, drop privileges before the upload: the network publish step does not need root, so re-exec the helper as the unprivileged service account rather than widening the sudo surface.

findings.title: deploy.yml pins actions/checkout to the mutable v4 tag while the release workflow pins the same action by commit SHA
findings.evidence:
The preview job resolves its checkout action from a floating tag: `- uses: actions/checkout@v4` (line 13). A git tag is a mutable pointer -- whoever controls the `actions/checkout` repository, or an attacker who compromises a maintainer account there, can repoint `v4` at a different commit, and every subsequent run of this workflow silently fetches and executes that new code. The identical action in the sibling workflow is pinned to an immutable object: `uses: actions/checkout@11bd71901bbe5b1630ceea73d27597364c9af683 # v4.2.2` (release.yml line 18), which is the repository's own declared standard for third-party action trust. The consequence is amplified here because this job runs with `permissions: write-all` (line 7) and, unlike the release job, does not set `persist-credentials: false`, so the action itself receives and stores a write-scoped GITHUB_TOKEN.

Independent validation: deploy.yml:13 pins actions/checkout to the mutable `v4` tag inside a workflow that runs on pull_request_target with permissions: write-all (lines 4, 7), so whoever can repoint that tag runs code with the base repo's write-all token - the documented tj-actions/changed-files class of attack, not a theoretical nit, which is why it survives rule 02 at LOW. Rule 13 untrusted writer: any maintainer of, or attacker with write access to, the actions/checkout repository. Rule 10: stripped release.yml:18 from code_paths - it is the hardened twin (commit-SHA pin, persist-credentials:false) and must not be flagged.

Production viability (VIABLE): The floating v4 tag is the shipped pin for a job that runs with write-all permissions, and the sibling release.yml pins the same action by commit SHA, establishing the repository's own standard.
findings.impact: A compromise of the upstream action repository, or of the tag alone, yields code execution in a runner holding a write-all GITHUB_TOKEN and this repository's secrets, with no change to any file in this repository and nothing in the diff for a reviewer to notice.
findings.recommendation: Pin by full commit SHA with a trailing version comment exactly as the hardened twin does at release.yml line 18 (`actions/checkout@11bd71901bbe5b1630ceea73d27597364c9af683 # v4.2.2`), add `persist-credentials: false` as that step does on line 20 so the checkout does not leave a write-scoped credential in .git/config, and enforce SHA pinning repository-wide (Dependabot with `versioning-strategy` on actions, or an allowlist policy in the org's Actions settings).
